concepts.title: Counting by One-to-One Mapping
concepts.definition: Before number names existed, herders counted by matching each object with one item of a standard sequence - a stick, a pebble, a notch or a sound - so that no two objects share the same marker; the final pile of markers answers questions about the size of a herd or a collection.
concepts.key_idea: A fixed-order sequence of markers (sticks, tally marks, letters) plus one-to-one pairing is all counting needs.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp103.txt lines 70-160 (mechanism of counting, methods 1-3), 302-330 (tally marks)

solution_steps.action: choose a standard sequence of markers
solution_steps.explain: Sticks, notches on bone, or sounds in fixed order can all serve as the sequence.

solution_steps.action: pair each counted object with one marker
solution_steps.explain: The pairing must be one-to-one: distinct objects get distinct markers in order.

solution_steps.action: compare marker piles to answer questions
solution_steps.explain: Missing cows, fewer-than comparisons and how-many-more questions all reduce to comparing the marker collections.

concepts.title: The Roman Number System and Its Limits
concepts.definition: Europe counted for centuries with Roman numerals built from symbols I, V, X and more, combining them additively and with subtraction rules like IV for 4; the system has no place value, so writing ever larger numbers keeps demanding new symbols.
concepts.key_idea: Roman numerals lack a base: each jump in size needs a fresh symbol, unlike place-value systems.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp103.txt lines 138-176 (method 3, Table 1), 660-664 (contrast with base systems)

solution_steps.action: split the number into landmark chunks
solution_steps.explain: Roman writing groups by ten, five and one using I, V, X and their higher symbols.

solution_steps.action: apply the subtraction rule where needed
solution_steps.explain: A smaller symbol before a larger one subtracts, as in IV and IX.
Without place value, larger sizes require additional symbols, which is the system's main limit.

concepts.title: Egyptian Base-10 Landmark Numbers
concepts.definition: The Egyptian system around 3000 BCE grouped collections by landmark numbers, each ten times the previous one, so the landmarks are the powers of 10; a number is written by counting how many of each landmark it contains, starting from the largest landmark below it.
concepts.key_idea: 324 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 4: group by powers of ten from the top.
question_patterns: represent 10458 in the Egyptian base-10 system

why is each Egyptian landmark number ten times the previous one

solution_steps.explain: Divide by the third landmark to get how many hundreds the number holds.
The leftover after removing hundreds is split into tens.
Whatever remains after tens is written in units.

concepts.title: Base-n Systems and Their Landmark Numbers
concepts.definition: Any positive integer n can drive a number system: start the landmarks at 1 and obtain each next landmark by multiplying by n, so the landmarks are n to the power 0, n to the power 1, n to the power 2 and onward; base 10 is the decimal system and grouping by 5 gives a base-5 system with landmarks 1, 5, 25, 125, ...
concepts.key_idea: Landmark numbers of a base-n system are the powers of n: for base 5 they are 1, 5, 25, 125, 625, 3125.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp103.txt lines 602-660 (base-5 system, landmark powers), 656-660 (definition of base-n)
question_patterns: compute the landmark numbers of a base-7 system

solution_steps.action: raise the base to the position
solution_steps.explain: The k-th landmark of a base-n system is n to the power k, counting from 0.

concepts.title: Expressing Numbers in Base-5
concepts.definition: To write a number in base-5, peel off the landmarks from the largest down: divide by 125, then by 25, then by 5, recording each quotient as the count of that landmark; 143 becomes one 125, three 5s and three 1s.
concepts.formula: groups125 = number // 125; rem = number % 125; groups25 = rem // 25; groups5 = (rem % 25) // 5; units = number % 5
concepts.key_idea: 143 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1: successive division gives each landmark's count.
question_patterns: express 143 in the base-5 system by grouping landmarks

solution_steps.explain: Divide the number by the largest landmark 125.

solution_steps.action: carry the remainder to the 25 landmark
solution_steps.explain: The leftover divides by 25 to give the count of 25s.
The remaining amount is grouped by 5 and the final remainder is the unit count.

concepts.title: Journey of the Hindu Numerals
concepts.definition: Number names on powers of ten appear in the Yajurveda Samhita; the ten digits with zero as a dot surface in the Bakhshali manuscript, Aryabhata explains scientific computation with ten symbols, Al-Khwarizmi and Al-Kindi carry the system to the Arab world around 800 CE, and Fibonacci persuades Europe around 1200 CE - which is why Europeans long called them Arabic numerals.
concepts.key_idea: The digits 0-9 are an Indian invention transmitted through the Arab world to Europe.
question_patterns: where did the digits 0 to 9 that we use today originate

solution_steps.explain: Yajurveda names by powers of ten; Bakhshali manuscript writes ten digits with a dot for zero; Aryabhata formalises computation.
Around 800 CE the system reaches the Arab world via Al-Khwarizmi and Al-Kindi.
Fibonacci's advocacy around 1200 CE spreads the numerals in Europe, where the mislabel Arabic numerals arose.
